Moreover, compared with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), VCTE has limited sensitivity for quantifying subtle changes in hepatic steatosis, particularly when steatosis is below 20%, but its low cost and portability are essential for translating public health research into large-scale practice. A weight reduction (>5%) has been shown to lead to steatosis remission in adults, with 10% needed for fibrosis improvement. Our study observed a 6.5% reduction in BMI Z score, correlating with liver steatosis and fibrosis improvement. However, BMI explained a limited proportion of the improvement in CAP, suggesting that other factors might have contribution to the intervention effect, such as improved dietary quality, increased physical activity, and metabolic changes including better insulin sensitivity and lower triglycerides. Although the intervention showed some effect on LSM, no mediation effect for BMI was found, possibly due to the limited BMI change or short intervention duration. In contrast, ALT did not show significant inter-group differences. Given the relatively low baseline ALT levels across the intervention, there was minimal room for further reduction. Furthermore, reduction in hepatic fat content can occur independently of significant alterations in ALT, particularly when baseline ALT levels are not markedly elevated. Building upon the observed reduction of prevalence of MASLD, we translated these clinical improvements into long-term societal impacts using a health-augmented macroeconomic model. Our projections estimate cumulative economic gains of approximately 0.013% of GDP (¥694.96 billion) by 2050. Notably, this magnitude aligns with other population-level public health policies, falling between the projected gains of sugar-sweetened beverage taxation (∼0.0016% of GDP) and alcohol excise tax increases (∼0.034% of GDP), underscoring the substantial economic potential of early MASLD prevention. However, these health-economic findings must be interpreted as a scenario-based exploration rather than a definitive macroeconomic forecast. The model used national-level demographic and epidemiological parameters combined with effect sizes from a specific regional sample (Ningbo, China). Given the limited sample size and regional focus of the trial, extrapolating these results requires caution regarding real-world scalability. These estimates serve as a proof-of-concept for future cost-effectiveness studies. Second, regarding sustainability, although the one-year timeframe inherently captured the impact of the winter break, potential “behavioural wash-out” during the longer summer hiatus remains unassessed. To address these uncertainties, we conducted extensive sensitivity analyses adjusting for sex, income, and applying a conservative 62.5% disease persistence rate from childhood to adulthood ( , ). Results indicated that even under the most conservative assumptions, the intervention consistently generated positive economic returns (ranging from 0.003% to 0.017% of GDP). Thus, while local adaptation is necessary, the current evidence suggests that a nationwide rollout would likely generate meaningful and robust macroeconomic benefits. This study has several strengths. First, clinical nutritionists were involved in delivering dietary guidance, which helped translate weight management knowledge into practical skills, benefiting not only the students’ health but also dietary practices among parents and school cafeterias. Second, the purposely designed mobile application effectively facilitated timely and convenient communication among schools, nutritionists, and parents, aligning with the communication preferences of modern families. Third, the adequate sample sise and cluster-RCT design strengthen the reliability of our findings. A post hoc power analysis based on the observed effect sises suggested moderate to adequate statistical power ( , ). Fourth, the economic modelling suggests that interventions targeting childhood MASLD may bring considerable economic returns. Nonetheless, several limitations should be noted. First, this study focused on one city, Ningbo, and included six public primary schools in eastern China, the findings are likely generalisable to similar urban contexts, but should be cautiously extended to regions with different economic or medical conditions. Second, COVID-19 pandemic restrictions and an early winter break confined children to their homes, significantly reduced extra school-based MVPA in the intervention groups, which likely underestimate the effect sise in the intervention group. Third, due to the nature of the lifestyle intervention, blinding of participants was infeasible, which may introduce performance bias. However, this risk was mitigated by the use of objective primary outcomes and blinded outcome assessment. Finally, the intervention covered only one academic year, and longer-term sustainability of the observed effects could not be evaluated. This cluster-randomised trial demonstrated that an mHealth-assisted, multifaceted lifestyle intervention effectively improved in BMI, liver health, and metabolic outcomes among children with overweight or obesity. These findings support the incorporation of such interventions into national child health strategies, particularly for mitigating obesity and preventing non-communicable disease. Ultimately, this study highlights the potential of multifaced interventions to yield both immediate clinical benefits and substantial long-term macroeconomic gains. Nearly a decade later, it is clear that the mere availability of a cure is insufficient to bridge aspiration to reality. The discovery of direct‐acting antivirals (DAAs) transformed HCV infection from a disease managed over decades to one curable in 8 weeks with a daily oral regimen. Unfortunately, deployment of this cure remains suboptimal. The HCV care cascade defines sequential steps from screening and diagnosis, linkage to care, treatment initiation, ongoing monitoring, culminating in sustained virologic response (SVR) which signifies a cure. There is significant fracture in the continuum of care, with progressive attrition at each step. A large meta‐analysis found that among persons screened positive for HCV, only 62% attended their first care appointment, 41% initiated treatment, 38% completed treatment, and only 29% achieved cure [ ], highlighting the magnitude of this problem. The emergency department (ED) serves as a vital access point for patients and encounters a higher prevalence of HCV infections compared to other care settings [ ]. Given the frequency with which HCV‐infected individuals interact with the ED, re‐conceptualising the care cascade to integrate screening and treatment initiation within this setting, could represent a crucial step toward addressing this public health challenge. This manuscript proposes a pragmatic framework for ED‐based HCV elimination within the United States healthcare system. The challenges and solutions described reflect the structure of U.S. care delivery, payer models and regulatory conditions. It may not directly translate to settings with different coverage or access constraints. The framework is intended to highlight the need for region‐specific strategies to address gaps in the care cascade. Five domains are addressed: point‐of‐care diagnostics, simplified treatment initiation and eligibility screening, policy and financial barriers, operational considerations and post‐treatment surveillance. The proposed pathway from ED presentation to SVR confirmation is summarised in Figure . 2 Point of Care Testing Innovations A critical requirement for any ED‐based model is the ability to establish a definitive diagnosis during the encounter itself. Point of care (POC) POC HCV RNA testing offers solutions to current, often cumbersome diagnostic pathways. Many facilities currently use a two‐step testing process: an initial antibody screening via rapid or lab‐based immunoassay, followed by confirmatory RNA testing if positive. These assays are conducted in separate laboratory sections, such as immunology and molecular diagnostics, or sent to external reference laboratories [ ], creating turnaround times on the order of days. POC fingerstick testing delivers results in ~1 h [ ], allowing diagnosis to be made within the critical window of opportunity where patient retention is most practical and intervention can be initiated promptly. Multiple studies have demonstrated strong diagnostic performance for these platforms [ , ]. On June 27th 2024, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration granted market authorisation to the first of these products [ ]. The ability to perform and interpret these tests without training in laboratory techniques makes them ideally applicable in ED settings. Widespread implementation, however, would require solutions to existing cost barriers. The Global Fund has successfully negotiated pricing and procurement agreements with Cepheid, the developer of the only FDA‐approved POC HCV RNA test to subsidise the cost of its tuberculosis testing products. Expansion of these agreements to include HCV testing products should also be pursued. Negotiation of bulk pricing by state or federal agencies, provision of subsidies for departments implementing these tests and advocacy for universal coverage of POC HCV RNA testing under Medicaid, Medicare, and private insurance are reasonable funding considerations. 3 Simplified Treatment Initiation The initiation of DAAs by non‐specialist providers may seem intimidating, and the concern is not unfounded. Expecting ED physicians to counsel patients on DAA side effect profiles, recognise drug interactions, and independently navigate serologic and fibrosis workups is a genuine cognitive burden in an already compressed clinical environment. Experience from other settings, however, suggests this barrier is surmountable when the right infrastructure surrounds the clinician. The HepCCATT study demonstrated meaningful improvement across the HCV care cascade. This was not achieved by training physicians to function as hepatitis C specialists. Instead, it relied on embedding ECHO‐Chicago tele‐mentoring support and providing frontline clinicians with expert backup [ ]. Critically, HepCCATT also illustrates the ceiling of workforce training alone. Despite gains in screening and diagnosis, only 7.7% of confirmed cases were ultimately treated. This finding underscores that individual clinician capacity is not the binding constraint. In the proposed ED model, this limitation is addressed through a different approach. EHR‐embedded clinical decision support (CDS) automates eligibility assessment, reflex laboratory ordering, and DAA prescription generation, reducing the physician's role to confirming eligibility and overriding the system when clinical judgement requires it. On June 11th, 2025, the FDA approved an expanded indication for glecaprevir/pibrentasvir (Mavyret), making it the first and only oral, pan‐genotypic, 8‐week regimen for the treatment of acute HCV in patients ≥ 3 years without or with compensated cirrhosis [ ]. This decision, grounded in the findings of the M20‐350 trial, further strengthens the rationale for ED‐based treatment models. While most cases of acute HCV infection are asymptomatic, up to 20% of individuals develop clinically apparent illness, often severe enough to prompt evaluation in the ED [ ]. However, the majority of HCV diagnoses made in the ED represent undiagnosed chronic infection. Distinguishing between these two is often clinically impossible. The stronger argument for ED‐based treatment rests not on the acute indication but on the well‐established efficacy of glecaprevir/pibrentasvir. The ED encounter however brief, represents a rare and often unrepeatable opportunity for intervention. Supporting this simplified treatment paradigm is the MINMON trial, which enrolled even compensated cirrhotics and HIV‐infected individuals with suppressed viral loads. Adopting a minimalist strategy, researchers omitted pre‐treatment genotyping, scheduled office visits, laboratory monitoring and dispensed the entire treatment course (84 tablets) to participants on enrolment. 91% of participants completed the 84 tablet course, SVR rate was 95% and safety was exceptional with no adverse events necessitating treatment discontinuation or death [ ]. The pragmatic approach of MINMON suggests that DAAs can be dispensed from the ED both safely and in a manner that delivers strong value for societal resources. Particularly compelling were SVR rates, which rival those reported in large outpatient and real‐world DAA cohorts [ ]. 4 Eligibility and the Minimal Safety Screen Based on the updated HCV test‐and‐treat algorithm, treatment can be safely initiated during an ED encounter in patients who are DAA‐naïve, not known to be HBsAg‐positive, have no history of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), and who lack clinical features of decompensated cirrhosis (ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, jaundice, or varices) [ ]. In this model, each of these criteria is operationalised within the ED encounter through EHR‐embedded CDS to reduce cognitive burden on ED clinicians. 5 Hepatitis B Virus Status Before DAA initiation, consideration must be given to coinfection with HBV owing to potential for seroconversion or HBV viral reactivation during therapy [ ]. Standard protocols involve assessing serum HBsAg, anti‐HBs, and anti‐HBc prior to DAA therapy initiation to assess whether a patient is immune to HBV, previously exposed, or actively infected. To alleviate cognitive burden on ED physicians, EHR‐based CDS tools should prompt these HBV serologic tests when HCV RNA positivity is confirmed, with reflexive ordering if results are not previously documented. A similar automated workflow has been successfully implemented in EDs, reflexing HCV RNA testing for positive HCV antibody testing on the same specimen [ ]. Those HBV‐immune from vaccination [HBsAg (−), anti‐HBc (−), anti‐HBs (+)] can proceed with ED‐based DAA initiation without additional precautions. This duration and monitoring burden is fundamentally incompatible with a single‐encounter treatment model. 6 <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">HIV</styled-content> And Antiretroviral Interactions While MINMON supports DAA initiation in HIV positive individuals, caution is required. The central concern is that of pharmacologic interaction between DAA regimens and antiretroviral therapy (ART). The proposed model addresses this by stratifying HIV patients into three operational tiers. Patients with documented HIV virologic suppression on a compatible ART regimen may proceed with ED‐initiated DAA therapy. Compatibility can be determined automatically through EHR‐embedded interaction checks. Those with viral suppression but on an interacting ART regimen are not started on DAAs in the ED. They are flagged for expedited referral to an infectious disease specialist. Patients with unsuppressed or undocumented HIV viral load are deferred from ED‐initiated treatment owing to the degree of clinical complexity such management entails. 7 Renal Impairment Renal impairment warrants brief consideration given its high prevalence in the ED population and relationship with HCV. HCV infection promotes renal disease through various mechanisms including membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, direct cytopathic injury to podocytes and tubular cells, and cryoglobulinemia [ ]. An internal inconsistency exists within current AASLD/IDSA guidance. While instruction regarding renal impairment endorses DAA therapy without dose adjustment across all CKD stages, the simplified treatment algorithm excludes patients with eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . It reflects historic caution around sofosbuvir's metabolite GS‐331007 which is renally cleared and putatively associated with cardiac toxicity in animal models [ ]. Contemporary data supports the safety and efficacy of both sofosbuvir and glecaprevir/pibrentasvir regimens in advanced CKD and dialysis [ ]. In the current proposed model, ESRD is not an exclusion. Patients with eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 who otherwise meet criteria proceed with glecaprevir/pibrentasvir, whose biliary clearance removes renal pharmacokinetic concerns. 8 Cirrhosis and Hepatocellular Carcinoma The early DAA era furnished signals suggesting accelerated hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) occurrence/recurrence after therapy, particularly in those with cirrhosis or prior history of HCC [ ]. Contemporary consensus holds that DAA treatment in cirrhotic patients reduces long‐term HCC risk compared to untreated cirrhosis but does not eliminate it [ ]. Ongoing surveillance therefore remains necessary. Decompensated cirrhosis further complicates treatment selection. NS3/4A protease inhibitor‐containing regimens are contraindicated due to impaired hepatic metabolism and the risk of drug accumulation. Instead, management requires sofosbuvir‐based regimens with ribavirin, introducing monitoring demands that are incompatible with a simplified low‐touch framework. Cirrhosis exclusion in the ED is operationalised through a combinatorial assessment of FIB‐4 and ultrasonography (USG). In the context of HCV infection, a FIB‐4 of < 1.45 has a negative predictive value exceeding 90% for ruling out advanced fibrosis [ , ]. Patients with FIB‐4 score elevated above this threshold or sonographic features of cirrhosis (surface nodularity, splenomegaly, ascites) would be ineligible for ED‐initiated treatment and should be triaged to expedited specialist referral. FIB‐4 requires only AST/ALT and the patient's age which are already routinely obtained in ED evaluation. Formal USG is available in most US ED's, particularly those affiliated with hospitals where radiology services are staffed. In rural hospitals or freestanding EDs, imaging acquisition is typically performed locally with interpretation support through teleradiology. Together, these modalities represent an immediately implementable cirrhosis exclusion strategy. History of HCC is addressed through history taking and EHR review at the time of eligibility determination. Patients with known prior HCC would also be excluded and referred. Soon, formal USG may be replaced with transient elastography. Palm‐sized wireless systems capable of B‐mode imaging and liver stiffness measurements have been developed, clinically validated [ ], and have already crossed FDA regularly threshold as of February 2024. Patients excluded from ED‐initiated DAA therapy whether due to HBsAg positivity, decompensated cirrhosis, unsuppressed HIV viremia, a history of HCC or complex drug interactions represent the highest risk individuals within the HCV‐infected population. For these patients, an appropriate response is a distinct, high‐priority active case management protocol, modelled on the infrastructure of the CDC's Perinatal Hepatitis B Prevention Program (PHBPP). The PHBPP is a currently functioning nationally funded programme in which HBsAg positivity in the specific clinical context of pregnancy triggers active case management rather than passive surveillance. This entails proactive outreach, household contact tracing, needs assessment, care coordination and eliminates patient self‐navigating and follow‐up [ ]. Spanning 2009 to 2017, the PHBPP case‐managed 100,372 infants born to HBsAg‐positive women across 56 jurisdictions, and over this time, increased timely administration of post‐exposure prophylaxis rates from 94.7% to 97%. Similar improvements were recorded for post‐vaccination serologic testing which increased from 58.8% to 66.8% ( p = 0.002), ultimately declining perinatal transmission from 0.9% to 0.4% ( p = 0.0006) [ ]. However, the PHBPP does not map perfectly to the ED HCV context. The heterogeneity of ineligibility criteria, absence of a third party harm imperative (i.e., risk of harm to a neonate), and lack of a dedicated federal funding mechanism represent important structural differences. It does however establish a key principle. A clearly defined high risk clinical trigger can justify an active case management infrastructure rather than passive referral. Applying this principle to treatment‐ineligible ED HCV patients would ensure that exclusion from the simplified pathway consistently initiates proactive specialist referral and coordinated follow‐up, rather than discharge with instructions alone. 10 Policy & Systemic Barriers A review of publicly available Medicaid HCV coverage policies across all 52 U.S. jurisdictions reveals a heterogeneous and frequently restrictive policy landscape (Table ). As of 2025, 18 jurisdictions (35%) require prior authorisation for initial DAA therapy, including most states that have not expanded Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act. In these settings, 62% of non‐expansion jurisdictions maintain prior authorisation requirements compared with 24% of expansion states. Prescriber restrictions persist in 12 jurisdictions (23%), ranging from “specialist‐only” mandates to continuing medical education (CME) based credentialing requirements. Substance‐use related requirements remain in 6 jurisdictions (12%), now uniformly framed as counselling attestation rather than sobriety mandates. Taken together, at least one barrier directly relevant to DAA‐naive patients presenting to the ED is present in 24 jurisdictions (46%). (Table ) Therefore, approximately half of U.S. Medicaid programmes would require additional policy navigation before the proposed model could be implemented without modification. Additionally, seven jurisdictions (14%) exhibit Managed Care Organization (MCO) parity gaps in which private insurance companies that administer Medicaid benefits on behalf of the state impose more restrictive HCV coverage criteria than the state fee‐for‐service programme. Given that a majority of Medicaid beneficiaries in most states are enrolled in MCOs rather than fee‐for‐service [ ], parity gaps represent a particularly insidious form of access restriction. The full state‐by‐state policy data are reported in Table . Feasible ED‐based HCV treatment initiation will therefore require targeted policy interventions alongside clinical implementation. Although prior authorisation removal has been shown to increase treatment rates [ ], abrupt universal rollback is a financially non‐viable strategy for most payers given anticipated surges in treatment demand. A more durable approach would be advocacy for ED‐specific prior authorisation exemptions. A useful precedent is noted in the liberation of buprenorphine prescription requirements during the COVID‐19 pandemic. Prior to 2020, the Ryan Haight Online Pharmacy Consumer Protection Act of 2008 required an in‐person evaluation before prescribing controlled substances via telemedicine. Removing a categorical prescribing barrier in a defined clinical setting can expand access without compromising safety. A structured ED‐based protocol can justify exemption from requirements that were designed for routine outpatient care. 11 Financial Access Barriers and Mechanisms for Cost Mitigation DAA therapies are now significantly more affordable than their initial entry into the HCV treatment armamentarium. When introduced in 2013, sofosbuvir was priced at $1000 per pill, totalling $84,000 for an 8 week course. Yet, meaningful cost barriers persist across insurance strata and are most acute precisely where HCV burden is highest. Patients with commercial insurance may have out‐of‐pocket costs as little as $5/month. However, patients relying on Medicare Part D historically faced average out‐of‐pocket costs approaching $5351 prior to recent legislative reforms, while uninsured individuals continue to encounter list prices for generic regimens ranging from $22,000 to $36,000 [ ]. The Inflation Reduction Act sought to ease this burden by implementing a $2000 annual cap and closing the long‐problematic coverage gap, which left patients exposed to substantial coinsurance after initial benefits [ ]. While these provisions are now in effect, recent policy shifts under the current administration introduce some uncertainty regarding the broader trajectory of federal drug pricing reform. This magnitude of cost is not driven by the complexity of drug manufacturing. Generic price modelling that incorporates active pharmaceutical ingredient costs, excipients, and production in India at a 10% profit margin estimates that a full course of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir can be produced for approximately $85 [ ]. In contrast, wholesale acquisition prices for preferred generic regimens have historically exceeded $20,000 per course, with no universal cost mitigation mechanism available outside insured and 340B‐eligible settings [ ]. These realities illustrate that cost barriers to HCV elimination in the United States stem from modifiable regulatory and policy constraints. One promising mechanism to offset DAA costs in the ED is the federal 340B drug pricing programme. If HCV treatment is prescribed and dispensed through an ED affiliated with a 340B‐eligible Disproportionate Share Hospital, medications can be acquired at steeply discounted prices. These savings may be passed on through sliding‐scale pricing or free dispensing to qualifying uninsured patients. Even in rural areas without owned outpatient facilities, 340B pricing can be accessed via contract pharmacy arrangements. While few existing bridge clinic models explicitly leverage 340B pricing, this presents an opportunity for innovation. EDs affiliated with 340B‐eligible hospitals could explore partnerships with nearby pharmacies to extend discounted DAA access beyond the ED encounter. Operationalising this model would require integrated electronic health record systems and dedicated care navigators. The federal 340B Drug Pricing Program offers a potential solution, but its reach is limited by structure. Under 340B, covered entities can purchase outpatient medications at significantly reduced prices. These savings can be passed on to uninsured or underinsured patients, potentially reducing DAA costs. Eligibility is uneven however. Rural critical access hospitals, freestanding emergency centres, and many community hospitals do not qualify. These are often the same settings where uninsured patients are concentrated. Even within eligible institutions, passing savings to patients depends on local policy and is not guaranteed or mandated [ ]. In addition, contract pharmacy arrangements, which have extended 340B pricing into community settings, face ongoing legal challenges following manufacturer restrictions introduced in 2020. This creates additional uncertainty, particularly for rural implementation strategies [ ]. For institutions outside the 340B system, no reliable same‐encounter cost mitigation mechanism currently exists for uninsured patients. Manufacturer patient assistance programmes, including AbbVie's myAbbVie Assist, offer free medication to qualifying uninsured patients but require income documentation, provider attestation, and a processing timeline of days to weeks. Addressing this gap will require policy‐level solutions: expansion of 340B covered entity eligibility, federal bulk purchasing mechanisms, or Medicaid expansion in the 13 states where uninsured adults below poverty remain categorically ineligible. A synthetic control analysis of Medicaid prescription data found that Louisiana experienced a 534% increase in HCV prescription fills following implementation [ ]. Despite this, neither state reached its elimination targets, indicating that improving affordability alone is not sufficient. These findings highlight the need for both care delivery and financial access reform. 12 Operational Considerations Beyond regulatory and financial prerequisites, feasibility depends on workflow integration within an already capacity constrained environment. Integrating HCV treatment into ED workflows adds modest physician workload if tasks are appropriately distributed. Serologic and radiographic tests run passively within the existing visit and physician involvement is limited to eligibility confirmation and prescription authorisation which are achievable in minutes with EHR‐embedded CDS. The downstream burden of patient counselling, insurance verification, prior authorisation navigation, and follow‐up coordination is best assigned to pharmacists and care navigators. Phlebotomy access warrants specific attention in persons serving PWID where poor venous access can extend intake time and impede concurrent patient management [ ]. Phlebotomy support and POC fingerstick compatible assays should be incorporated where available. Staffing requirements for ED‐based HCV initiation have not been prospectively defined and will likely vary by institution. Estimates depend on expected RNA positivity rates, the proportion of patients who meet simplified treatment criteria, and the non‐physician workload required per patient. Data from outpatient programmes provide a useful reference point. The Boston Medical Center primary care HCV programme reported annual staffing costs of $282,770, corresponding to approximately $940 per patient referred and $4160 per SVR [ ], with most of the workload carried by non‐physician staff. Across implementation studies, a consistent finding is that successful programmes require protected and dedicated time for pharmacists and care navigators. Dispensing logistics will vary by institutional context. Large urban emergency departments affiliated with health systems that have on‐site pharmacies offer the most straightforward implementation pathway. In these settings, EHR‐based screening alerts, co‐located pharmacist or navigator support during clinical shifts, and in‐house dispensing can function as a fully integrated model. When an on‐site pharmacy is unavailable, partnerships with community pharmacies provide a practical alternative. Electronic prescription transmission with same‐day or next‐day dispensing can preserve the central goal of minimising the gap between diagnosis and treatment initiation. Rural emergency departments operate under different constraints, including lower patient volumes, limited specialist access, and smaller staffing models. A hub‐and‐spoke telehealth approach is a reasonable adaptation. Point‐of‐care testing and eligibility screening can be performed locally, while treatment evaluation and authorisation are completed through real‐time telemedicine consultation. Although same‐visit dispensing may not always be feasible in this setting, same‐visit eligibility determination with rapid electronic prescribing and pharmacy dispensing within 24–48 h still represents a meaningful improvement over current pathways that often result in no treatment. 13 Post‐Treatment Surveillance and Cure Confirmation SVR12, defined as an undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks after treatment completion, is the accepted endpoint of cure and the target for post‐treatment follow‐up. For patients started on therapy in the ED, reaching this endpoint depends on two steps. A confirmatory sample must be obtained, and the result must be delivered to a patient who may no longer be connected to traditional care. Dried blood spot testing offers a practical solution for sample collection. A simple fingerstick applied to filter paper avoids venipuncture, does not require refrigeration, and remains stable for months [ ]. This allows collection in settings where these patients already engage, including harm reduction sites, opioid treatment programmes, and needle exchange services. For patients with stable housing, mail‐in or community drop‐off options can eliminate the need for a return visit altogether. In real‐world settings, dried blood spot testing has shown high accuracy, with reported specificity of 100% and sensitivity approaching 96% [ ]. There are limitations. Variability in sample volume, drying conditions, and processing can affect reliability at very low viral levels, where false negatives are the main concern [ , ]. When feasible, venous sampling remains preferred, but dried blood spot testing is an appropriate alternative when it is not. The second challenge is ensuring that results reach the patient and that non‐responders are identified. Telemedicine has shown benefit, with studies demonstrating improved SVR rates and engagement compared to standard referral pathways [ , ]. However, its reach is limited in the same populations that rely on the ED. Access to smartphones, stable internet, and the ability to attend scheduled visits cannot be assumed. Simpler approaches may be more reliable. Asynchronous text messaging programmes have been associated with improved adherence and reduced treatment‐related distress in VA‐based HCV programmes [ ]. For patients without dependable digital access, in‐person follow‐up through harm reduction or opioid treatment programmes remains essential. Reinfection should be anticipated in populations with ongoing injection drug use. SVR does not confer immunity, and recurrence is not uncommon. This does not represent treatment failure. Reinfection can be managed with the same DAA regimens, with preserved efficacy. The appropriate response is retreatment alongside renewed engagement in harm reduction services. Follow‐up encounters for SVR confirmation provide an opportunity to reassess risk, reinforce counselling, and link patients to treatment for opioid use disorder when appropriate. No single follow‐up strategy will reach all patients. Effective post‐treatment care requires flexibility and selection of the approach that best fits the individual. 14 Conclusion This framework represents a deliberate shift in how the HCV care cascade is approached. Rather than relying on delayed linkage to outpatient care, it begins at the point of ED contact. Point‐of‐care RNA testing, simplified eligibility assessment, same‐visit treatment initiation, decentralised SVR confirmation, and flexible follow‐up together form a model grounded in the realities of the populations most affected by hepatitis C, particularly those with inconsistent access to traditional care. The barriers are real. Regulatory requirements vary across states. Financial access remains uneven and, in some settings, legally contested. Staffing these programmes requires institutional investment that cannot be secured through a single policy change. These constraints do not undermine the model. They define the areas where advocacy, pilot implementation, and prospective evaluation should be focused. Hepatitis C is curable. The tools to diagnose infection within an hour, treat it in weeks, and confirm cure without a clinic visit already exist. What remains is a delivery system that continues to lose patients at each step. The downstream consequences of cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and their socioeconomic burden rest like an anvil on the healthcare system. Addressing this will require more than incremental change. It will require rethinking where and how care is delivered. The emergency department is not traditionally designed for chronic disease management, but for a condition defined by silent progression and concentrated among patients who rely on the ED for care, it may be the most consequential place to intervene. Highlight box Key findings • A prognostic nomogram was developed and validated to predict 3-, 6-, and 12-month cancer-specific survival (CSS) in patients with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma lung metastasis (ICCLM). • The nomogram-based risk score effectively stratified patients into low- and high-risk groups with significantly different survival outcomes. What is known and what is new? • Patients with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma generally face low survival and high risk of recurrence, with overall survival rates of approximately 30% and 18% at 1 and 5 years, respectively. • This study establishes a population-based prognostic model integrating age, liver metastasis, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy to enable individualized survival prediction in ICCLM patients. In our study, the 1-, 3-and 5-year CSS rates for patients with ICCLM were 23.9%, 3.3% and 0.8%, respectively, with a median CSS of 5 months. What is the implication, and what should change now? • The nomogram provides refined risk stratification beyond conventional staging systems, allowing clinicians to identify patients with relatively favorable versus extremely poor prognosis. • Low-risk patients may be considered for active multimodal treatment strategies, including systemic therapy and selected locoregional approaches. • For high-risk patients with very limited predicted survival, the model may assist in avoiding overtreatment, prioritizing non-surgical management, and facilitating early palliative care planning. Introduction Primary liver cancer (PLC) predominantly comprises three histological subtypes: hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (ICC), and mixed HCC-ICC ( ). ICC is an epithelial malignancy arising from the biliary epithelium, accounting for 10% to 15% of PLC and ranking as the second most common histological subtype after HCC ( , ). In recent years, the incidence and mortality rates of ICC have increased globally ( , ). Unfortunately, the prognosis for ICC patients, whether surgical or non-surgical, remains unsatisfactory ( ). Even post-curative surgery, the 5-year overall survival (OS) fluctuates between 20% and 35%, coupled with a high recurrence rate spanning 40% to 80% ( , ). As the disease progresses, advanced ICC may metastasize to extrahepatic organs, with the lungs being the most common site of distant organ metastasis ( , ). Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma lung metastasis (ICCLM) distinctly differs from other tumors, necessitating its own unique prognostic prediction model. An effective prediction model can assist clinicians in tailoring the optimal treatment strategy for individual patient prognoses. The traditional tumor-node-metastasis (TNM) staging system primarily focuses on tumor size, lymph node metastasis, and distant metastasis, overlooking other patient attributes such as age, gender, and treatment methods ( , ). As a result, the TNM staging system might not be wholly applicable to all ICC patients, especially those in advanced stages with distant metastasis. There is an urgent need for a more precise staging system tailored for ICCLM patients. The nomogram is a practical and ideal visualization tool for predicting and calculating the outcome probabilities for each patient and has been extensively utilized in aiding clinical decisions ( , ). Given the relative rarity of ICCLM patients, we employed the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database to study a cohort of ICCLM patients from 2010 to 2020. This research aimed to develop a nomogram to predict cancer-specific survival (CSS) rates for these patients, which subsequently underwent both internal and external validation. The findings suggest that this nomogram can offer clinicians enhanced prognostic prediction, risk stratification, and a valuable tool for clinical decision-making. We present this article in accordance with the TRIPOD reporting checklist (available at https://tcr.amegroups.com/article/view/10.21037/tcr-2025-2083/rc ). Methods Patients and data selection Utilizing the SEER*Stat software (version 8.4.2), we extracted clinical-pathological data and prognostic information of ICC patients from the SEER database spanning the years 2010 to 2020. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and its subsequent amendments. Given that SEER operates as a de-identified public database, there was no requirement for patient informed consent or ethical approval. Our analysis was conducted in strict adherence to the guidelines set by the SEER database. The clinical variables collected encompassed: year of diagnosis, age, sex, race, marital status, histological grade, tumor stage, surgical interventions, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, liver metastasis, bone metastasis, and brain metastasis. The primary endpoint of this study was the CSS, defined as the duration from the date of diagnosis to the date of death attributed to the cancer. Inclusion criteria were as follows: (I) diagnosis year between 2010 and 2020; (II) ICD site code: C22.1; (III) international Classification of Diseases for Oncology, Third Edition (ICD-O-3) code 8160. Exclusion criteria encompassed: (I) patients diagnosed via autopsy or death certificate; (II) patients with missing pivotal clinicopathological data, such as age, sex, race, marital status, histological grade, and tumor stage; (III) unknown information regarding surgical interventions, chemotherapy, or radiotherapy; (IV) undetermined distant metastasis data (bone, brain, liver); (V) ambiguous cause of death; (VI) indeterminate survival duration; (VII) presence of primary tumors in other locations. In this study, a total of 620 ICCLM patients were included. Patients diagnosed between 2010 and 2017 were randomly divided into a training cohort (70%) and an internal validation cohort (30%). Patients diagnosed between 2018 and 2020 were defined as the external validation cohort ( ). During follow-up, a total of 537 CSS events were observed in the entire cohort. As the final multivariable Cox regression model included 4 independent predictors, the events per variable (EPV) ratio was 134.3, which supports the robustness of our multivariable analysis. Statistical analysis In this study, we constructed a nomogram using a training cohort (n=274) and subsequently validated the model with both an internal validation cohort (n=118) and an external validation cohort (n=228). Assisted by the X-tile software, we identified 50 and 70 years as the optimal age cut-off points. For prognostic factors, univariate Cox regression analysis was initially employed to screen relevant variables. Subsequently, the variables with P<0.10 were incorporated into a multivariate Cox regression analysis, leading to the identification of independent prognostic factors associated with ICCLM. We constructed the ICCLM prognostic model using the RMS package in R software. Following this, the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve of the nomogram was plotted, and its discriminative ability was evaluated using the area under the curve (AUC). Through ROC curve analysis, the discriminative power of the nomogram was compared with that of other independent risk factors. Additionally, calibration curves and decision curve analysis (DCA) were generated to further assess the model’s performance. Ultimately, based on the median risk score, all patients were stratified into high- and low-risk groups. The predictive value of the nomogram was validated using survival curves and the log-rank test. All statistical analyses were conducted in R software version 4.3.1, with P<0.05 considered statistically significant. Results Characteristics of ICCLM patients From the SEER database, we identified 1,238 patients diagnosed with ICC accompanied by lung metastasis (LM) between 2010 and 2020. After applying the aforementioned exclusion criteria, 618 patients were excluded, resulting in a total of 620 patients included in this study. Of these, 392 patients diagnosed between 2010 and 2017 were randomly allocated into a training cohort (n=274) and an internal validation cohort (n=118) at a 7:3 ratio. Patients diagnosed between 2018 and 2020, totaling 228, were designated as the external validation cohort. The baseline clinical, pathological, and specific characteristics of the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts are summarized in . Within the training set, age stratification was performed using the X-tile software (version 3.6.1), revealing that 56.6% of patients were in the age range of 50–70 years. The majority of patients were Caucasian and married. In terms of sex distribution, 55.5% were male and 44.5% were female. Regarding tumor characteristics, Grade III tumors accounted for 21.9%, but notably, a significant portion of the data was categorized as “unknown”. The most common T and N stages were T2 (54.4%) and N1 (54.7%), respectively. Among these patients, 42 (15.3%) had bone metastasis, 93 (33.9%) had liver metastasis, and only 1 (0.4%) had brain metastasis. In terms of treatment modalities, the vast majority of patients (98.5%) did not undergo surgical intervention, 174 patients (63.5%) received chemotherapy, and 24 patients (8.8%) underwent radiotherapy. Prognostic factors for ICCLM patients To assess various prognostic factors, we conducted both univariate and multivariate Cox regression analyses ( ). The results from the univariate Cox regression analysis indicated that age, marital status, brain metastasis, liver metastasis, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy were significantly associated with prognosis (P<0.10). However, factors such as sex, race, histological grade, T stage, N stage, and bone metastasis showed no statistically significant correlation with prognosis. The multivariate Cox regression analysis further identified age, liver metastasis, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy as independent prognostic factors for CSS. Prognostic nomogram development and validation We included all independent risk factors and developed nomograms using the RMS package in R software to predict the CSS of ICCLM patients at 3-, 6-, and 12-month ( ). As depicted by the nomogram, chemotherapy statistically emerged as the most significant factor influencing CSS, followed by age, radiotherapy, and liver metastasis. The C-indices for the training cohort, internal validation cohort, and external validation cohort were 0.723 [95% confidence interval (CI): 690–0.756], 0.761 (95% CI: 0.714–0.770), and 0.758 (95% CI: 0.719–0.797), respectively, confirming the high predictive accuracy of the prognostic model. Further, we compared the AUC values across different cohorts ( ). For the SEER training cohort, the AUC for predicting 3-, 6-, and 12-month CSS were 0.818 (95% CI: 0.765–0.870), 0.788 (95% CI: 0.735–0.848), and 0.753 (95% CI: 0.699–0.819), respectively. For the internal validation cohort, the AUC for 3-, 6-, and 12-month CSS were 0.846 (95% CI: 0.767–0.917), 0.853 (95% CI: 0.775–0.921), and 0.804 (95% CI: 0.704–0.896), respectively. For the external validation cohort, the AUC for 3-, 6-, and 12-month CSS were 0.852 (95% CI: 0.795–0.925), 0.777 (95% CI: 0.716–0.849), and 0.763 (95% CI: 0.692–0.840), respectively. Compared to predictions based on individual prognostic factors, the nomogram exhibited superior accuracy in predicting CSS at 3-, 6-, and 12-month ( ). Additionally, calibration curves for the 3-, 6-, and 12-month CSS were plotted for each cohort, showcasing a high degree of consistency between the nomogram predictions and actual observations ( ). Lastly, the DCA curves for all three cohorts further underscored the clinical utility of the nomogram ( ). The Nomogram consistently demonstrated a superior net benefit over the “treat none” (illustrated by the blue line) and “treat all” (illustrated by the green line) strategies across most probability thresholds. Establishment of a risk stratification system based on the nomogram model In our study of 620 patients, KM survival analysis revealed survival rates of 23.9%, 3.3%, and 0.8% at 1-, 3-, and 5-year, respectively, with a median CSS of 5 months ( ). Utilizing the Cox proportional hazards model, we calculated scores for each independent prognostic factor, culminating in a composite risk score for each patient. Subsequently, risk stratification was established based on the median composite risk score across the three cohorts. Our findings consistently indicated that patients in the high-risk group exhibited significantly lower CSS than those in the low-risk group across training, internal validation, and external validation cohort ( ). Within the training cohort, the survival rates for the high-risk group at 3-, 6-, and 12-month were 24.0%, 10.6%, and 3.9% respectively, while those for the low-risk group were 78.6%, 78.6%, and 37.0%. Discussion Surgical resection is considered the only potentially curative treatment for ICC patients. Regrettably, due to the insidious and non-specific early symptoms of ICC, the majority of patients are diagnosed at an advanced stage ( ). As a result, the resection rate for ICC remains low, with a poor prognosis, and the OS rates at 1- and 5-year are approximately 30% and 18%, respectively ( , ). In fact, distant metastasis is a hallmark of advanced ICC, indicating a poor prognosis for patients. It is well known that the TNM staging system primarily focuses on tumor size, lymph node metastasis, and distant metastasis, yet it overlooks other pivotal patient characteristics such as age, sex, and treatment modalities ( , ). Hence, the TNM system might not be entirely appropriate for all ICC patients, especially those with distant metastases. Therefore, it becomes imperative to develop a system that can accurately predict the prognosis of ICCLM. Notably, Shi et al. ( ) constructed nomograms to predict the likelihood of lung and bone metastases in ICC patients at diagnosis. However, no study has yet developed a validated prognostic tool tailored to patients who already present with ICCLM. In this study, we analyzed the baseline demographic and clinical characteristics of the patients. To identify independent prognostic factors, we conducted both univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazard regression analyses. The univariate analysis suggested that age, marital status, brain metastasis, liver metastasis, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy are potential prognostic indicators for patients with ICCLM. Upon multivariate analysis, only age, liver metastasis, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy emerged as independent prognostic factors. A nomogram was subsequently constructed based on these four factors. The model was validated using the C-index, ROC curves, calibration curves, and DCA curves demonstrating good accuracy and high reliability. KM survival curves revealed a significant difference in CSS between the low- and high-risk groups, underscoring the practicality of our model. In summary, the nomogram accurately predicts the 3-, 6-, and 12-month CSS for ICCLM patients. It has been reported that the incidence of ICC increases with age, with a median patient age of 62 years ( - ). The prognosis is typically unfavorable when ICC is accompanied by intrahepatic metastasis ( ). Research by Shi et al. ( ) highlighted that intrahepatic metastasis is a primary factor leading to LM in ICC patients. Consistently, our study found that ICC patients with concurrent liver and lung metastases have a poorer prognosis. Radiotherapy and chemotherapy both hold pivotal roles in tumor treatment ( ). Patients with distant metastases are typically recommended for systemic treatments, such as systemic chemotherapy and targeted therapy ( ). Among these, the combined chemotherapy regimen of gemcitabine and cisplatin is considered the most effective first-line treatment strategy for ICC patients with distant metastases ( , , ). Radiotherapy has also been demonstrated to prolong the survival of ICC patients and reduce the risk of death from tumor-related liver failure ( - ). In our study, both chemotherapy and radiotherapy demonstrated a positive correlation with patients’ survival rates. Further, multivariate analysis revealed that chemotherapy significantly contributes to the survival of ICCLM patients. In a retrospective study on ICC with brain metastasis, the median survival time was found to be only 3.7 months, with patients exhibiting advanced T-stage, untreated primary lesions, lack of radiotherapy, and presence of bone metastases showing unfavorable prognoses ( ). Yuan et al. ( ) also highlighted that the TNM stage is an independent risk factor affecting the prognosis of ICC patients. However, it’s imperative to note that our study specifically focuses on stage IV ICCLM patients. Upon analyzing the prognosis of ICCLM patients, we found that Grade stage, T-stage, N-stage, surgical resection, bone metastasis, and brain metastasis did not constitute independent prognostic factors, which was consistent with our previous studies of patients with bone metastases from ICC ( ). In discussing the indications for surgical resection of distant ICC metastases, Yoh et al. ( ) suggested that surgery is a reasonable option for patients with intrahepatic metastasis, vascular invasion, or regional lymph node metastasis, as long as a complete resection is feasible upon gross examination. Yan et al. ( ) found that for patients with isolated liver metastases, surgery at the primary site (P=0.002) and at the metastatic site (P=0.005) both conferred survival benefits. However, for patients with isolated pulmonary metastases, only surgery at the metastatic site showed a survival advantage (P=0.01), while surgery at the primary site did not demonstrate significant benefits. It is worth noting that given the subjects we studied, the number of patients choosing surgery was relatively small. In conclusion, further research is warranted to validate the therapeutic outcomes of surgery in such patients. In many cancers, nomograms have been demonstrated to be more accurate and user-friendly than traditional staging systems ( , ). Our nomogram ultimately incorporates easily obtainable factors (age, liver metastasis, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy), facilitating individualized calculations for ICCLM patients. Notably, the impact of chemotherapy on CSS was the most significant, with patients undergoing chemotherapy exhibiting higher CSS than those not receiving chemotherapy. In assessing the robustness of our model for predicting CSS across various time intervals, the training cohort, internal validation, and external validation cohorts consistently demonstrated satisfactory predictive performance, with AUC values consistently exceeding 0.75. The C-indices for the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts were 0.723, 0.761, and 0.758, respectively. A higher C-index generally indicates more accurate prognostic predictions ( ). This suggests that our nomogram offers a high degree of authenticity and reliability in predicting CSS in ICCLM patients. While our study offers valuable insights, there are several noteworthy limitations. Firstly, the data for this research was solely derived from the SEER database, implying that the findings might not be entirely representative of regions outside the United States, such as Asia, Africa, and South America. Moreover, the SEER database lacks data on certain factors that could be closely associated with prognosis, such as hepatitis B virus (HBV) or hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections, carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9) levels, and vascular invasion. Thirdly, our external validation data also originated from the SEER database, which might influence the robustness of the validation. Finally, our study used complete-case analysis, excluding approximately 50% of the initial cohort due to missing T and N staging data—a potential source of selection bias if missingness relates to disease severity or treatment access. Although statistical power was sufficient (EPV >100), generalizability may be limited by this non-random attrition. Conclusions We constructed and validated a line chart for predicting 1-, 6-, and 12-month CSS in ICCLM patients. Our proposed diagram takes into account four independent risk factors: age, liver metastasis, chemotherapy and radiotherapy. After internal and external verification, it shows good accuracy and clinical applicability, which can help clinicians to implement individual clinical decisions. INTRODUCTION Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is still a challenge of global public health, particularly in the Asia-Pacific region [ ]. Long-term outcomes of HBV infection can be significantly influenced by concurrent liver conditions, notably hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) [ - ]. These dual pathologies are increasingly recognized as critical modifiers of HBV-related liver disease progression, treatment response, and overall prognosis. Understanding the similarities and differences in how HCV and MASLD impact HBV-infected individuals is essential for guiding appropriate clinical management. EPIDEMIOLOGY OF HCV AND MASLD IN SUBJECTS WITH CHRONIC HBV INFECTION Chronic HBV infection affects over 290 million individuals globally, with the highest burden concentrated in Asian countries [ , ]. In these endemic areas, HBV is often acquired during the perinatal period or early childhood, leading to a high rate of chronic infection [ , ]. While the prevalence of HCV varies regionally, it remains an important coexisting infection in populations at risk for parenteral transmission, for example, people who inject drugs, patients receiving transfusions before blood screening implementation, and individuals with human immunodeficiency virus co-infection [ - ]. Historically, HBV/HCV coinfection has been observed in the Asia-Pacific region before the global implementation of HBV vaccine program and blood product screening [ - ]. In Taiwan and parts of mainland China, earlier studies reported that up to 1% of the population carried both viruses, often due to superinfection with HCV in individuals with hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) carriage [ ]. However, in recent years, HBV/HCV coinfection rates have declined due to universal infant HBV vaccination, public health campaigns, and the introduction of direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapies highly effective for the cure of HCV [ ]. In contrast, MASLD has become the most common liver disease in the world, affecting an estimated 25–30% of the global population, with rising incidence across both developing and developed countries [ - ]. This trend is closely linked to the growing prevalence of obesity, sedentary lifestyles, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. In Asia, the burden of MASLD is expanding rapidly. For instance, the prevalence of MASLD in urban Chinese adults rose from approximately 13% in 2003 to over 40% by 2016 [ , , - ]. In South Korea, rates have increased from 19% to 27% within a decade [ , , ]. Among subjects chronically infected with HBV, the co-existence of MASLD is becoming increasingly common, though reported prevalence varies widely from 15% to over 50%, depending on population characteristics and diagnostic methods ( ) [ - ]. Interestingly, several studies suggest that chronic infection with HBV may be associated with hepatic steatosis in an inverse way, although this observation remains controversial and may be influenced by metabolic parameters of the host [ , , , ]. Nonetheless, with the global rise in metabolic syndrome (MetS), the burden of dual HBV/MASLD is expected to grow, warranting careful attention in clinical management and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) surveillance programs [ , ]. CLINICAL INSIGHTS FROM HBV AND HCV COINFECTION Declining prevalence and incidence due to public health policy and the introduction of potent DAA therapy HBV and HCV coinfection presents complex challenges for diagnosis, treatment planning, and long-term outcome prediction [ - ]. Either cohort or case-control studies have demonstrated that the clinical outcomes are worse in patients with HBV/HCV coinfection compared to those with mono-infection by either virus [ , ]. Specifically, coinfected individuals are at greater risk for accelerated liver fibrosis, decompensation, and development of HCC [ ]. These adverse outcomes underscore the need for proactive treatment strategies. The implementation of global HBV vaccination programs—starting with the World Health Organization’s 1992 recommendation—has significantly reduced new HBV infections and, by extension, the incidence of new HBV/HCV coinfection [ , ]. In parallel, the availability of highly efficacious DAAs for HCV has made viral eradication including HBV/HCV coinfection a feasible goal in nearly all patients [ , ]. What happens during anti-HCV therapy if we only target HCV? Antiviral therapy in coinfected subjects requires particular caution. Interferon-based regimens such as pegylated interferon (peginterferon) with ribavirin were previously used and showed durable HCV eradication and, in some cases, concurrent reductions in serum HBsAg titers [ - ]. More recently, DAA-based treatments have already become the standard of care for HCV and have demonstrated satisfactory sustained virological response, even in HBV coinfected subjects [ , ]. An unexpected concern is the risk of HBV reactivation (HBVr) following peginterferon- or DAA-induced HCV clearance [ - ]. In subjects with dual liver diseases, the interactions between two etiologies can be quite complex [ ]. For example, for subjects coinfected with HBV and HCV, HCV infection has been found to suppress HBV replication [ ]. In subjects with dual liver diseases, the interactions between two etiologies can be quite complex [ ]. For example, for subjects coinfected with HBV and HCV, HCV infection has been found to suppress HBV replication [ ]. With the advent of potent DAA agents that achieve rapid and sustained eradication of HCV, clinicians began observing an unintended consequence: HBVr [ , , ]. HBVr typically manifests as a sudden rise in HBV DNA levels, often accompanied by reappearance or increase of HBsAg, and in some cases, biochemical hepatitis flares [ ]. The underlying mechanism is thought to involve loss of HCV-mediated immune control, particularly through diminished hepatic interferon signaling [ ]. In a multicenter cohort study from Taiwan, HBVr occurred in up to 70% of HBsAg-positive subjects after DAA therapy for HCV, although only 10–15% developed clinically significant hepatitis [ , ]. Most reactivations occurred during or within 12 weeks after the completion of DAA therapy. In severe cases, especially those with underlying cirrhosis, HBVr has led to hepatic decompensation and even liver failure [ , ]. Retrospective studies and case series have also confirmed HBVr risk across various DAA regimens [ , ]. Importantly, HBVr appears to be less common in subjects with isolated anti-HBc (HBsAg-negative) or in those who are inactive HBV carriers with undetectable or low serum HBV DNA [ ]. What can we do to prevent HBVr? Due to the potential for severe liver outcomes, international guidelines—including those by AASLD and EASL—recommend that all subjects scheduled for DAA therapy undergo HBV screening [ , ]. For those with active HBsAg positivity, prophylaxis with nucleos(t)ide analogue (NUC) should be considered starting with DAA therapy and continued for at least 12–24 weeks after its completion [ , ]. A Taiwanese randomized trial demonstrated that entecavir prophylaxis during DAA therapy markedly reduced the risk of HBVr [ ]. In patients who received entecavir starting with DAAs, HBVr was reduced from over 60% (no prophylaxis group) to 0%, with no hepatitis flares or liver failure. This finding strongly supports the implementation of antiviral prophylaxis in high-risk subjects. Surveillance of HCC after eradication of HCV in the HBV/HCV coinfected subjects HCC surveillance in HBV/HCV-coinfected subjects post-HCV cure is an important concern in clinical practice. Even after HCV eradication, persistent HBsAg or pre-existing fibrosis warrants continued semiannual ultrasound, with or without alpha-fetoprotein monitoring per international society guidance for the development of HCC [ , ]. Lessons we learned from HBV/HCV coinfection In sum, while DAA therapy revolutionized HCV treatment, clinicians must remain vigilant in subjects with HBV coinfection (Box 1) [ ]. HBVr is common, preventable, and may be life-threatening. Prophylactic antiviral therapy and close post-treatment monitoring are critical components of safe and effective management. Unfortunately, HBV screening and prophylactic NUC use during DAA therapy remain inconsistent globally in clinical practice despite international guideline recommendations, and real-world registries show variable HBVr rates [ - , ]. Another lesson learned from these basic and clinical studies on HBV/HCV coinfection is that there is reciprocal interaction, usually suppressive effect, between two viruses. If the management plan of HBV-related dual liver disease only targets one etiology (HCV in this case) but leaves the HBV infection untreated, HBV may reactivate and potentially lead to severe clinical adverse events, including liver failure. Understanding the risk of HBVr in HBV/HCV coinfected subjects calls for attention to the potential risk of HBVr in other HBV-related dual liver diseases such as HBV/MASLD ( ). As MASLD becomes the dominant chronic liver disease in the 21st century, clinicians managing HBV must be equipped to assess, monitor, and address the metabolic contributors to liver injury (Box 2) [ ]. DEFINITION AND DIAGNOSIS OF COEXISTING STEATOTIC LIVER DISEASE AND MASLD IN SUBJECTS WITH CHRONIC HBV INFECTION Definition of steatotic liver disease and MASLD Steatotic liver disease (SLD), previously termed as fatty liver disease, is currently the most prevalent liver disorder globally [ , ]. This new nomenclature “SLD” was proposed in 2023 by the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases and the European Association for the Study of the Liver with the aim to avoid stigmatization of the affected subjects [ ]. Among SLD, MASLD is defined in patients who have SLD as well as the presence of at least 1 cardiometabolic risk factor [ ]. Non-invasive diagnosis of SLD, MASLD, and metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis The presence of hepatic steatosis (SLD) can be detected by non-invasive liver imaging study, for example, ultrasonography of the abdomen and computed tomography [ ]. The diagnosis of hepatic steatosis in subjects with HBV infection can be made with the help of various clinical models [ - ]. Beyond steatosis, distinguishing metabolic dysfunctionassociated steatohepatitis (MASH) and identification of fibrosis in subjects with HBV infection has also prompted the use of noninvasive algorithms [ , ]. INTERPLAYS AMONG HBV INFECTION, HEPATIC STEATOSIS AND MetS Prevalence of hepatic steatosis in subjects with HBV infection is related to MetS Several cross-sectional analyses suggest that subjects infected with HBV infection may exhibit lower rates of fatty liver in comparison with the general population or subjects with HCV infection [ , , , , - ]. The underlying mechanisms accounting for this observation are not fully clarified yet. To investigate how frequently hepatic steatosis occurs in HBV-infected populations within the Asia–Pacific region, Wong and colleagues conducted a study involving 91 individuals with HBV and 922 healthy controls in Hong Kong [ ]. They used magnetic resonance spectroscopy to quantify the content of fat in the liver, and demonstrated that HBV infection was a factor independently associated with a lower likelihood of hepatic steatosis. Only 13.5% of HBV-infected subjects exhibited steatosis as compared to 28.3% among controls (p=0.003). Clinically, individuals with coexisting steatosis are often overweight or obese, older in age, and tend to have hypertension and reduced physical activity levels—traits consistent with metabolic dysfunction [ , , , , - ]. Cross-sectional studies have consistently shown that hepatic fat accumulation in subjects with chronic HBV infection is more closely associated with features of MetS than with HBV infection itself. For instance, in a Taiwanese health screening cohort of 507 individuals—50 with HBV and 457 without—the presence of fatty liver and insulin resistance was not related to the status of HBV infection [ ]. Notably, these associations did not extend to HBV infection itself, underscoring the dominant role of metabolic abnormalities in driving steatosis within this patient population. Effects of hepatic steatosis and metabolic dysfunction on HBV replication and HBsAg seroclearance One of the most intriguing observations in subjects with chronic HBV infection is the potential inverse correlation between hepatic steatosis and the status of viral replication [ , ]. Several clinical studies have shown that HBV-infected individuals with concurrent steatosis often exhibit lower HBV DNA levels, reduced rates of HBeAg positivity, and higher frequencies of spontaneous HBsAg seroclearance [ , - ]. For example, in a large Taiwanese cohort of 4084 HBeAg-negative treatment-naïve subjects [ ], 887 individuals had coexisting hepatic steatosis. Compared to those without steatosis, these patients exhibited significantly lower serum HBsAg titer and lower serum HBV DNA titer. Over a median follow-up of five years, hepatic steatosis was found to be associated with a higher chance of achieving HBsAg seroclearance (the adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] being 1.43). Furthermore, the presence of individual metabolic dysfunctions showed a cumulative and additive effect on enhancing HBsAg clearance. Patients with hepatic steatosis also demonstrated a greater likelihood of HBsAg seroconversion (aHR 1.37) compared to their counterparts without steatosis. These results remained robust across multiple sensitivity analyses and persisted even after adjusting for virological and clinical parameters through inverse probability of treatment weighting. Collectively, these findings suggest that metabolic factors may not only influence disease progression but also facilitate favorable immunological outcomes in HBV infection including reduction in serum HBsAg level and even HBsAg seroclearance. The mechanisms underlying this phenomenon remain to be investigated [ - ]. In vitro studies suggest that hepatocyte lipid accumulation may impair HBV replication via induction of endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, autophagy disruption, or cytokine signaling alterations. Additionally, adipokines such as adiponectin and leptin may play immunomodulatory roles that influence HBV viral dynamics. Animal models support these findings. In HBV-transgenic mice fed with high-fat diets, investigators observed a marked suppression of viral markers, including reduction in serum HBsAg and HBsAg levels [ , ]. Similarly, in cellular models, lipid accumulation inhibited secretion of viral particles [ ]. These findings propose a theoretical model in which metabolic stress interferes with HBV persistence mechanisms. Impact of MetS on HBV-related fibrosis progression and hepatocarcinogenesis The contribution of MetS to HBV-related liver disease progression has been increasingly recognized. In a longitudinal study involving 663 untreated HBV-infected individuals, Wong et al. [ ] assessed the dynamic changes in MetS and their impact on hepatic fibrosis over a two-year period. Liver stiffness was measured at baseline and follow-up using transient elastography. During the observation window, the prevalence of MetS rose from 12% to 21%, with 13% of subjects developing new-onset MetS and 3% experiencing resolution. Notably, 16% exhibited fibrosis progression. Multivariate analysis identified coincidental MetS as an independent risk factor for fibrotic advancement, with an adjusted odds ratio of 2. These findings support the role of metabolic disturbances in exacerbating liver damage in HBV-infected individuals. MetS encompasses five key elements—diabetes, obesity, hypertriglyceridemia, hypercholesterolemia, and hypertension—but whether specific type or cumulative number of these abnormalities has a greater impact on hepatocarcinogenesis in subjects with chronic hepatitis B is still an open question. In a Taiwanese cohort of 1,690 men with HBV infection followed over a median period of 19 years [ ], individuals presenting with ≥3 metabolic abnormalities had significantly higher risks of HCC (hazard ratio 2.32) and liver-related mortality (hazard ratio 2.72). Similarly, a Canadian biopsy-based cohort of 1,850 CHB subjects revealed that those with MetS had a heightened risk of liver complications, especially among those with multiple concurrent metabolic comorbidities [ ]. Reinforcing these findings, a recent hospital-based study involving over 10,000 untreated CHB subjects in Taiwan found a clear dose-dependent relationship between the number of metabolic dysfunctions and the incidence of HCC, with type 2 diabetes mellitus emerging as the most prominent individual risk factor [ ]. Korean nationwide study also demonstrated that metabolic risk factors independently increased risk of HCC [ ]. Elevated total cholesterol level, triglyceride level, and low density lipoprotein level were linked to a lower likelihood of developing HCC in both the general population and HBV-infected individuals [ ]. However, these observations require confirmation through prospective studies and deeper mechanistic exploration to better understand this paradox. Cohort studies also demonstrated contradictory findings that use of statins was associated with lower HCC incidence in CHB patients [ - ]. Overall, HBV/MASLD is associated with a higher risk of hepatocarcinogenesis. Thus, HCC surveillance in HBV subjects with MASLD is recommended. However, in non-cirrhotic or younger (for example, those <40 years of age) populations, whether routine surveillance of HCC is costeffective remains uncertain and needs to be investigated in future cohort studies [ - ]. Intriguing role of simple hepatic steatosis in HBV-related liver disease progression Co-existing hepatic steatosis and MetS are common among subjects infected with HBV, yet their individual and combined contributions to HCC risk remain contentious. In a recent retrospective study collecting more than 10,000 treatment-naïve HBV patients, hepatic steatosis—observed in 21% of the cohort—was associated with favorable virological and biochemical profiles, such as lower HBeAg positivity rates, reduced serum HBV DNA levels, and a decreased Fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) index [ ]. During a median 5.1-year follow-up, hepatic steatosis emerged as an independent factor associated with a 60% reduction in HCC risk. Based on the same cohort, similar beneficial impact of simple steatosis was observed regarding the risk of allcause mortality and cause-specific mortality [ ]. After a median follow-up of 9.1 years, subjects with simple steatosis had a lower risk of mortality (hazard ratio 0.62) than those without MASLD. Among non-cirrhotic subjects with HBV infection, hepatic steatosis was associated with a lower risk of developing liver cirrhosis (aHR 0.57 within 5 years) and cirrhosis-related complications (aHR 0.45) [ ]. Notably, among individuals with SLD, the risk of developing cirrhosis was higher in subjects with co-existing metabolic dysfunction in comparison to those without metabolic dysfunction. Conversely, other studies have suggested adverse implications of steatosis. A Hong Kong-based cohort of 270 HBV-infected subjects who received liver biopsy found that 40% had biopsy-proven steatosis at baseline [ ]. These patients frequently exhibited features of metabolic dysfunction, advanced liver disease including cirrhosis, and genetic susceptibility linked to the PNPLA3 rs738409 CG/GG variant. Steatosis in this group independently increased HCC risk by over seven-fold during a 6.5-year follow-up. However, the presence of cirrhosis in over a quarter of these individuals at baseline limits generalizability to broader clinical settings. Meta-analyses have echoed these mixed findings [ , - ]. While some pooled analyses showed no significant link between hepatic steatosis and fibrosis or cirrhosis in CHB [ ], others reported a paradoxical inverse association between steatosis and HCC development [ ]. One individual patient data meta-analysis even found reduced risks of HCC, cirrhosis, and mortality in CHB patients with hepatic steatosis, along with higher rates of HBsAg seroclearance [ ]. These discrepancies likely reflect heterogeneity in disease severity across cohorts and call for more refined studies with clearly defined clinical subtypes. These complex dynamics underscore the need for careful risk stratification among subjects with dual HBV/MASLD, into those with versus those without coexisting MetS. Data from Taiwan’s cohorts clearly revealed that the presence of simple hepatic steatosis without metabolic derangement may be associated with favorable clinical and virologic outcomes [ , , , , ]. However, the presence of any metabolic derangement, especially type 2 diabetes, contributes to the development of HBV-related liver cirrhosis, HCC, and liverrelated mortality. Overall, although reduced viral replication may confer some benefits, this must be balanced against the detrimental hepatic effects of metabolic dysfunction [ , ].
