Medical management of PSC-IBD Management of stable IBD in PSC follows general IBD treatment principles. Immunomodulators ( e.g . azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine) are used both in moderate disease and in post-LT immunosuppressive regimens. Observational data suggest these agents may be associated with a reduced risk of acute cholangitis and longer IBD remission after LT. Conversely, anti-TNF therapy has been associated with an increased risk of acute cholangitis in PSC-IBD, raising concerns about its use in those with recurrent cholangitis as their transplant indication. Vedolizumab, a gut-selective anti-integrin, appears safer, with studies demonstrating clinical improvement in over half of treated patients, although it does not appear to modify the liver disease course or significantly improve liver biochemistry. Patients with PSC-IBD were not included in the seminal trials with the newer advanced therapies (IL-12/23, S1P, and JAK inhibitors), and the safety and efficacy of these therapies in PSC-IBD will be guided by emerging real-world data. Surgical considerations and timing of colectomy For patients with active or refractory IBD, especially those approaching LT, optimizing disease control is essential in keeping with IBD society guidelines. The decision to continue medical management vs . proceed to surgery should involve multidisciplinary input from gastroenterology, hepatology, and transplant teams. Active IBD at the time of LT is associated with worse graft outcomes and an increased risk of rPSC. A multicentre study found an increased hazard of rPSC in those with active disease post-LT (HR 1.7; 95% CI 1.08-2.75). The timing of surgery relative to LT should consider the urgency of transplant, severity of colitis, and presence of dysplasia or colorectal malignancy. The ESOT (European Society of Organ Transplantation) recommends a multidisciplinary approach and supports pre-transplant colectomy in select patients with refractory colitis or neoplasia. Patients with persistently active disease despite escalation may require colectomy prior to or at the time of transplantation, particularly if there is no contraindication from a portal hypertension perspective. Historically, the risk of rPSC was shown to be significantly less in those who undergo pre/peri-transplant colectomy (3.4%) than in those who undergo post-LT colectomy (43.8%), with meta-analysis demonstrating a lower hazard of rPSC in those who undergo pre-transplant colectomy (HR 0.65; 95% CI 0.42-0.99). However, a more recent international multicentre study did not find a significant difference in rPSC based on timing of colectomy in PSC-IBD (HR 1.57; 95% CI 0.54-4.6). The indication for colectomy influences the risk of rPSC. Medically, patients with refractory PSC-IBD have a higher incidence of rPSC and biliary complications than those undergoing colectomy for oncological indications. In those in whom colectomy is contraindicated due to clinically significant portal hypertension pre-LT, colectomy should be considered within 6 months post-LT ( ). Choice of surgical technique Ileal pouch anal anastomosis (IPAA) should be used cautiously in PSC-IBD due to an increased risk of pouchitis, particularly after LT, where chronic pouchitis has been reported in over 67% of cases. Colectomy with end ileostomy has consistently been associated with more favourable graft outcomes compared with IPAA; however, a recent multicentre study reported comparable graft survival between IPAA and end ileostomy. Ultimately, the surgical approach should be determined by a multidisciplinary team – including surgeons, hepatologists, and gastroenterologists – and take patient preferences into account, although we generally recommend avoiding IPAA in PSC-IBD. Listing considerations Graft options Donation after brain death (DBD) grafts are preferred in PSC due to superior graft survival and lower rates of ischaemic cholangiopathy. Multiple studies have shown that donation after circulatory death (DCD) grafts are associated with increased risks of graft failure and biliary complications, particularly ischaemic cholangiopathy. , , However, DCD may be reasonable in selected patients – such as those who are older, have a low MELD score, and are at low risk of prolonged ischaemia – when high-quality DBD grafts are unavailable. , , Optimal DCD outcomes depend on minimising donor warm ischaemia time and carefully selecting both donor and recipient. For patients with PSC, particularly younger or high-risk individuals, caution remains warranted when considering DCD grafts. Because MELD and its derivatives may underrepresent disease severity and disadvantage patients with PSC, living donor liver transplantation (LDLT) is an important option for eligible patients with an available donor. This can shorten waiting list

Because MELD and its derivatives may underrepresent disease severity and disadvantage patients with PSC, living donor liver transplantation (LDLT) is an important option for eligible patients with an available donor. This can shorten waiting list times and decrease waiting list mortality. , A large registry study identified reduced graft survival with LDLT compared to DCD and DBD. In a large multicentre study, post-LT survival was inferior with LDLT compared to DBD (HR 1.92; 95% CI 1.05-3.49), making DBD preferable if available. Special considerations need to be evaluated in concomitant PSC-IBD, as management can be challenging. In patients who have undergone bowel surgery before LT, adhesions, together with severe portal hypertension, may increase surgical risk. That said, a combined procedure of LT and total colectomy seems to be a viable option for patients with PSC-IBD. There is no definitive consensus on the ideal biliary reconstruction technique in LT for patients with PSC. Historically, many centres have preferred hepaticojejunostomy over duct-to-duct anastomosis due to the perceived lower risk of disease recurrence, biliary complications and de novo CCA. Duct-to-duct anastomosis restores the natural anatomy and function of the biliary tree, while maintaining normal Oddi sphincter function, and facilitates ERC access, which can be useful in the post-transplant period. Additionally, in patients with previous bowel surgery resulting in a shortened small bowel or small bowel oedema due to portal hypertension, hepaticojejunostomy may not be feasible. , However, it is not clear whether hepaticojejunostomy is superior to duct-to-duct anastomosis with respect to survival benefit. A meta-analysis showed that anastomotic bile leak rates, graft survival, PSC recurrence and de novo CCA were comparable between the two reconstruction techniques. However, hepaticojejunostomy seems to be associated with higher risks of acute cholangitis . The recent ESOT Consensus Statement , although with moderate quality of evidence, recommended that the choice of biliary anastomosis should be left to the surgeon; however, duct-to-duct anastomosis is recommended as the reconstructive technique of choice whenever technically feasible. Novel preservation technologies may abrogate the increased risks of post-transplant complications in patients with PSC. Ex situ machine perfusion, namely hypothermic oxygenated perfusion and normothermic machine perfusion, have both demonstrated the capacity to optimise graft assessment and selection, facilitate transplant logistics, and achieve improved clinical outcomes. , While machine perfusion may improve outcomes in patients with PSC, given its promising early outcomes, long-term evaluations of these techniques are still needed. Exception points Allocation of exception points varies by transplant centre and governing body. As MELD and its derivatives do not fully capture disease burden in variant transplant indications, exception points are awarded in some geographic areas to address clinical scenarios underrepresented by MELD. In the UK there is a national transplant waiting list, and the National Liver Offering Scheme was introduced in 2018 for elective DBD transplantation. This allocates organs according to the transplant benefit score, which incorporates recipient and donor characteristics, including aetiology of liver disease. For refractory pruritus and recurrent cholangitis, and for patients being considered under a new service evaluation of transplantation for an unresectable intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (≤2 cm) without extrahepatic disease and without underlying chronic liver disease, patients can be listed as having a variant syndrome and offered organs outside of the transplant benefit score according to waiting time. In Canada, exception point allocation remains highly variable across provinces. A recent survey revealed that four of five provinces grant exception points for recurrent cholangitis, typically based on frequency of hospitalisations and antibiotic use. Ontario is the only province with specific criteria for awarding points for refractory pruritus, while three provinces recognise CCA as an indication, with differing criteria and exception points awarded. The absence of national consensus creates regional disparities. In the US, the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network has developed detailed guidance for MELD exception review. For recurrent bacterial cholangitis, exception points may be approved when there are ≥2 documented hospitalisations within 6 months despite maximal medical therapy. For refractory pruritus, MELD exceptions can be considered when it significantly impairs quality of life and is unresponsive to medical therapy. Evidence of complications such as skin excoriations or sleep deprivation is often required. For early-stage perihilar CCA, standardised protocols ( e.g . the Mayo protocol) allow MELD exception listings, typically granting patients a starting MELD score of 22, with upgrades every 3 months. The tumour marker alpha-fetoprotein is measured every 6 months as part of HCC surveillance in patients with cirrhosis. Outside of the transplant waiting list setting, imaging surveillance of PSC is generally recommended by international guidelines, , but is somewhat controversial. A recent prospective study of combined clinical evaluation, tumour markers, and imaging evaluation failed to diagnose CCA early enough to improve survival. Imaging surveillance on the transplant waiting list is a distinct scenario and is also not guided by high-quality evidence. Imaging surveillance is guided by the indication for LT and symptom development. For example, patients who have received neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy prior to LT for CCA require close surveillance with 3-monthly contrast-enhanced cross-sectional imaging. Other factors to consider are local resources as well as the expected time on the LT waiting list. In the case of portal vein thrombosis identified on pretransplant assessment, active surveillance and management are critical. Cross-sectional imaging should be repeated every 3 months to monitor for clot regression, stability, or progression, and treatment should be guided by imaging findings ( i.e . continuation of anticoagulation alone vs . consideration of portal vein recanalisation with transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt placement). Overall, imaging surveillance is guided by the indication and symptom development, as is the case for patients with PSC who are not on the LT waiting list. Mental health Mental health is an essential part of patient management while on the LT waiting list. In a 2020 survey through PSC Support, 75% of respondents indicated that psychological support was very or extremely important on the waiting list, with 69% indicating they needed psychological support on the waiting list. Further, 54% experienced anxiety. A 2007 study identified that those on the LT waiting list had more depression and lower health-related quality of life compared to healthy controls. The 2007 study did not find a significant difference in mental health in those with chronic liver disease on or off the LT waiting list, supporting that mental health should be addressed while on the waiting list and as part of every clinic appointment, with psychological and psychiatric support offered. Patients can be directed to local accredited PSC support and information websites for reliable information. Nutrition and prehabilitation Physical frailty/sarcopenia contributes to adverse clinical outcomes before and after LT. The liver frailty index was developed for use in patients with cirrhosis in the ambulatory setting and is associated with waiting list mortality. Prehabilitation has been demonstrated to improve post-surgical outcomes and should be offered to patients. , Nutritional support is an integral part of LT care. Those with PSC, and particularly those with PSC with advanced chronic liver disease, are at increased risk of nutritional deficiencies, including fat soluble vitamin deficiencies (vitamins D, A, K, and E), calorie deficits, and macronutrient deficiencies (protein, fat, and carbohydrates). , Oral nutritional supplementation may be required to meet the recommended intake of 35-40 kcal/kg/day and 1.2-1.5 g/kg/day of protein and provide macronutrients. If these measures are insufficient, dietician involvement and enteral feeding should be considered. Rotating antibiotics Rarely, those with recurrent bacterial cholangitis may require long-term and rotating antibiotics. There is no strong evidence to support the use of rotating antibiotics in recurrent cholangitis. Use may increase the risk of multidrug resistance. Still, society guidelines acknowledge the role in select cases with expert multidisciplinary input to drive decision making and choice of antibiotic, considering sensitivity from microbiological samples, including biliary aspirates. Consequently, pruritus must continue to be managed while on the transplant waiting list. If pruritus worsens, relevant strictures should be investigated with cholangiography and balloon dilatation with brushings. Non-pharmacologic approaches begin with keeping nails short, using emollients, and avoiding hot showers and baths. Though liver disease is listed as a contraindication in the product monograph, we regularly prescribe bezafibrate for cholestatic pruritus in Child-Pugh A and B cirrhosis. We recommend use with caution in Child-Pugh C cirrhosis, particularly in those with progressive renal dysfunction. Bezafibrate should not be used when creatinine clearance falls <60 ml/min, though some decrease the dose to 200 mg with frequency guided by extent of renal dysfunction. We monitor creatinine kinase 1 month after initiation and repeat if symptoms of myopathy develop, including muscle weakness or pain. Rifampin, an activator of the pregnane X receptor (PXR), is effective but requires monitoring for hepatotoxicity. In a large retrospective cohort study of rifampin-associated hepatotoxicity in patients treated for cholestatic pruritus, fewer than 5% developed hepatotoxicity. Of the five who did, two had index bilirubin >2.5 mg/dl. AASLD primary biliary cholangitis guidance suggests avoiding rifampin in those with a bilirubin >2.5 mg/dl. , In some who do prescribe above this threshold, co-prescription of vitamin K can be given to reduce the risk of coagulopathy. With weekly monitoring of liver tests due to variable drug metabolism, we prescribe rifampin in decompensated cirrhosis. In those without cirrhosis and those with compensated cirrhosis, we monitor liver enzymes every 1-4 weeks for the first 3 months after initiation and discontinue if alanine aminotransferase rises to more than 5 times the upper limit of normal. The half-life of rifampin is approximately 2-3 h. As rifampin is a strong CYP 3A4 inducer, medication interactions should be reviewed prior to initiation. Immediate post-transplant calcineurin inhibitor levels may be increased due to rifampin use. Opioid antagonists ( e.g ., naltrexone) and the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor sertraline may be helpful, but the evidence is modest and mostly derived from small or uncontrolled trials. , Historically naltrexone was avoided in those with cirrhosis due to concerns regarding hepatotoxicity. However, in a large retrospective cohort study of those with compensated and decompensated cirrhosis and alcohol use disorder, naltrexone was shown to be safe. The half-life of naltrexone is 4-13 h. Dosing should start at 12.5 mg daily with up-titration every 3-7 days to a maximum of 50 mg per day. , , Naltrexone should not be given in those with concurrent opioid use. Further, as opioids are likely to be used as part of a post LT pain management strategy, alternative anti-pruritic medications should be considered. For patients already stabilised on naltrexone, anaesthesiology should be engaged at listing to plan opioid alternatives for intra- and postoperative pain management. Sertraline accumulates in the setting of hepatic impairment. In those with Child-Pugh A or B cirrhosis, sertraline should start at a low dose of 25 mg with slow titration up by 25 mg each time and no sooner than every 2 weeks to a maximum dose of 100 mg. Sertraline is advised against in Child-Pugh C cirrhosis. Sertraline may increase bleeding risk due to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor-induced platelet serotonin depletion. Bile acid sequestrants are occasionally used ( e.g . cholestyramine), though there is insufficient evidence in PSC, and their tolerability and palatability are limited. Ursodeoxycholic acid UDCA increases the hydrophilic pool of bile acids, stabilises cell membranes, inhibits apoptosis, and improves bile flow. If a patient is stable and tolerating low-intermediate dosing, there is insufficient evidence to support either continuation or discontinuation during LT assessment and listing. In general, there is robust evidence to support the role of UDCA in improving liver biochemistry. , , , However, meta-analyses have not demonstrated improvement in survival, prevention of CCA, disease progression, nor symptom improvement with UDCA. , , , A large Japanese retrospective cohort study of 325 patients with PSC identified improvement in transplant-free survival with low-dose UDCA. However, the UDCA monotherapy group was younger (mean age 45.8 compared to 52.5), had less occurrence of symptoms (34% compared to 40%), and had lower FIB-4 (1.14 compared to 1.98) than the untreated group at baseline. These estimates were not directly statistically compared as the Japanese study included a bezafibrate group and a combination bezafibrate/UDCA group, and all comparisons were omnibus tests. These estimates were not directly statistically compared as the Japanese study included a bezafibrate group and a combination bezafibrate/UDCA group, and all comparisons were omnibus tests. EASL guidance indicates UDCA can be used at 15-20 mg/kg/day with available data not allowing for a firmer recommendation. AASLD guidelines note UDCA can be considered after 6 months of observation prior to assessing if ALP and gamma-glutamyltransferase spontaneously normalise. Higher doses (28-30 mg/kg/day) should be avoided due to their association with worse outcomes including development of varices, need for LT, and death. Further, higher doses are associated with colonic neoplasia in those with PSC-IBD. Still, the pathogenic mechanisms of bile acids in the colon remain unclear and these adverse associations have not been observed at low or medium doses. In our centres, UDCA is not initiated after listing; however, if a patient is already taking UDCA without side effects, it is continued. Post-transplant management Risk of disease recurrence In a recent systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 studies, the pooled prevalence of rPSC was 17.7%. A large French national cohort study of 571 patients from 1985-2019 reported an rPSC rate of 25.9%, with 5-, 15-, and 25-year recurrence risks of 15.6%, 37.9%, and 52.6%, respectively. The diagnosis is based on histologic (fibrous cholangitis and/or fibro-obliterative lesions with or without ductopenia, biliary fibrosis, or biliary cirrhosis) or imaging findings typical of cholangiopathy 90 days or more post-LT, after excluding alternative causes of biliary strictures (including hepatic artery ischaemia, DCD cholangiopathy, ABO incompatibility, ductopenic rejection, and cytomegalovirus). , The presence of refractory IBD, CCA pre-LT, recurrent cholangitis as the indication for LT, advanced donor age, acute cellular rejection, cytomegalovirus, and increased systemic inflammatory states, both before and after, have been identified as risk factors for rPSC. , Periductal infiltration with IgG4 cells in the explant is associated with increased risk of rPSC and shorter time to re-transplant. Recently, a study including Canadian and UK cohorts demonstrated that the development of cholestasis within 3-12 months following LT was predictive of rPSC and graft loss. There is no role for protocol biopsies, though abnormal liver biochemistry should prompt liver biopsy if clinically indicated. As rejection is associated with rPSC, rejection should be promptly acted upon with histologic confirmation and treatment initiation. Cross-sectional imaging should be performed to evaluate the hepatic artery and bile duct anatomy in the setting of cholestatic liver enzyme elevation. As described above, the role of colectomy pre-LT is an ongoing topic of study, though it has been associated with rPSC. Active management of IBD should remain a priority post-LT to decrease the risk of rPSC. Though rare, de novo CCA can develop in those with rPSC. , , Our local practice is to perform annual MRCP once rPSC has been diagnosed, to identify the rate of progression of cholangiopathy, targets for biliary intervention and areas suspicious for CCA. There are no approved disease-modifying therapies to decrease the risk of rPSC. There is insufficient data to support the use of UDCA after LT, with a large French cohort demonstrating UDCA had no impact on rPSC risk. We do not start UDCA for prevention of rPSC. However, in those who develop rPSC with elevated ALP, a trial of 15-20 mg/kg/day can be given and continued if biochemical improvement is observed. PSC recurrence is associated with the need for repeat LT, with the European Liver Transplant Registry demonstrating increased odds of re-transplant in those with rPSC compared to those without rPSC (odds ratio 3.6; 95% CI 2.7-4.8). Further, this large registry identified worse graft and overall survival in those with rPSC, though this impact was altered by timing of recurrence, with better graft survival in those who were diagnosed with rPSC 5 years after LT (15-year graft survival of 38% in those diagnosed with rPSC within 5 years compared to 51% in those diagnosed after 5 years). Mortality at 90 days is similar for patients undergoing re-LT for rPSC compared with other indications; however, mortality at 5 years is significantly lower. Due to the increased risk of rPSC associated with T cell-mediated rejection, some centres favour an enhanced immunosuppression strategy; however, there is a great deal of variability across centres. Induction with basiliximab and/or steroids is recommended. The backbone of long-term immunosuppression post-LT for PSC is tacrolimus. Post-transplant immunosuppression There is no universally agreed immunosuppression strategy post-LT for PSC, and the choice should be individualised. Due to the increased risk of rPSC associated with T cell-mediated rejection, some centres favour an enhanced immunosuppression strategy; however, there is a great deal of variability across centres. Induction with basiliximab and/or steroids is recommended. The backbone of long-term immunosuppression post-LT for PSC is tacrolimus. Tacrolimus is the preferred calcineurin inhibitor, as it offers superior long-term patient and graft survival compared to cyclosporine. However, tacrolimus was associated with rPSC, independent of IBD activity and previous colectomy, in a large multicentre study. In this study, however, low dose steroids were part of the immunosuppression strategy. Other large studies have not identified a similar association. , Use of steroids has been associated with rPSC in multivariate analysis; however, it is unclear whether this reflects active IBD or rejection, both of which are independent risk factors for rPSC. Univariate analysis in a large cohort study identified steroid use as an independent risk factor for rPSC (HR 2.22; 95% 1.49-3.31). Corticosteroids should be tapered early unless there are overlap features with autoimmune hepatitis. , Adjunct therapies, including mycophenolate and azathioprine can be used and tapered after the first year. Mycophenolate is associated with a decreased hazard of rPSC (HR 0.62; 95% CI 0.41-0.92); however, after adjustment for covariates, this association was no longer statistically significant. In our centres, tacrolimus is the preferred first-line option for immunosuppression. Post-transplant IBD management A systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 studies identified that in those with intact colons at the time of LT, IBD improved in 29.4%, remained unchanged in 51.4%, and worsened in 25.2% post-LT. The cumulative incidence of an exacerbated -post-LT IBD course was 0.22. Active IBD at the time of LT is associated with worse post-LT disease course. Management of IBD should be undertaken in collaboration with specialist IBD and transplant hepatology teams. Biologics and small molecules are effective for the treatment of IBD after LT. , , However, biologic therapy in combination with standard post-LT immunosuppression is associated with increased infection risk, particularly with Clostridioides difficile . Further, in a multicentre study, 17% of patients on anti-TNF after LT developed colorectal cancer, supporting vigilant post-LT annual colonoscopies in those with PSC-IBD. In those without PSC-IBD at LT, there should be a low threshold to investigate for IBD after LT if symptoms develop, as de novo IBD can develop after LT (26.2% of patients without IBD at time of LT developed IBD over a median time of 11.7 years in a US-based cohort). Data on optimal post-LT immunosuppression in PSC-IBD are conflicting. The use of tacrolimus and mycophenolate have been independently associated with increased IBD activity after LT. , , However, these findings are not consistent across studies. Azathioprine, and the combination of azathioprine and cyclosporin are associated with decreased risk of IBD activity after LT. , , In PSC-IBD, we prefer azathioprine over mycophenolate. Due to improvement in graft and overall survival, tacrolimus remains the mainstay of immunosuppression. Risk of post-transplant malignancy Patients transplanted for PSC are at risk of de novo malignancies after transplant with a 10-year cumulative incidence of cancer of 18.7%. The most common malignancies after transplant for PSC are post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD), renal cell carcinoma, and colon cancer. The immunosuppressive regimens were not significantly different between patients with PSC and cancer and those without; however, the immunosuppression intensity have not been directly compared. PTLD risk is linked to greater intensity of immunosuppression, so a judicious balance of immunosuppression is a priority, acknowledging that T cell-mediated rejection is associated with rPSC. Clinical screening for signs and symptoms of PTLD should be performed at each clinical visit. Apart from standard age-based cancer screening and regular skin surveillance there is no clear guidance on who and how to screen for post-transplant malignancies. In a systematic review and meta-analysis, colon cancer risk after LT for PSC was 5.8 per 1,000 person-years. This incidence markedly increased in those with PSC-IBD and an intact colon to 13.5 per 1,000 person-years. Dysplasia was more common in patients who developed rPSC after transplantation (54% of those with dysplasia had rPSC compared to 38% who did not develop dysplasia). Surveillance with colonoscopy should continue annually after transplant in patients transplanted with PSC-IBD. Conclusion In conclusion, LT remains the only definitive treatment for PSC. Given the progressive nature of the disease and the risk of complications, prognostic scores can be valuable in identifying patients at increased risk of decompensation or adverse outcomes. These can help guide the decision to proceed with LT. The main indications for LT in PSC include decompensated cirrhosis, cholangiopathic complications (including recurrent cholangitis and refractory pruritus), and CCA in selected programmes. While MELD and its derivatives are widely used for assessing liver transplant eligibility, they do not always fully capture the severity of PSC, especially in patients with variant LT indications. In such cases, exception points should be considered to more accurately reflect the disease burden and provide a mechanism for successful LT. As the landscape of PSC management evolves, further standardisation of transplant referral criteria and MELD exception pathways is critical to improve equity and access to LT. Multidisciplinary and personalised care involving the patient, hepatology, gastroenterology, radiology, and transplant surgery remain essential – particularly in the management of PSC-IBD. Future research should prioritise prospective studies aimed at personalising transplant referral and listing strategies, clarifying optimal PSC-IBD management, refining post-LT immunosuppressive strategies to mitigate recurrence, and exploring the role of PSC-specific prognostic scores in transplant listing. Upfront surgical resection without percutaneous biopsy is recommended, as biopsy carries risks of tumor seeding and low diagnostic yield in myxoid lesions. Alt-text: Unlabelled box dummy alt text Introduction Undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma of the liver (UESL) is a rare and aggressive mesenchymal tumor, first recognized as a distinct entity by Stocker and Ishak in 1978 [ ]. It is the third most common primary malignant liver tumor in children, after hepatoblastoma and hepatocellular carcinoma, typically affecting those aged 6-10 years [ , ]. UESL rarely occurs in adults, with a mean age of 24 years in reported cases, and carries a more aggressive course and poorer prognosis due to delayed diagnosis and therapeutic challenges [ , ]. Imaging plays a critical role in diagnosis, but features are often nonspecific and discordant across modalities, leading to misdiagnosis in up to 23.5% of cases [ ]. This case report highlights the multimodal imaging characteristics of UESL in a young adult and emphasizes the importance of multidisciplinary evaluation for timely management. Case report A 23-year-old woman, otherwise fit and well, presented with a 6-week history of right upper quadrant pain. Physical examination revealed tender hepatomegaly without jaundice or signs of chronic liver disease. Laboratory investigations, including liver function tests and tumor markers (alpha-fetoprotein [AFP], CA19-9, carcinoembryonic antigen), were unremarkable. Serology for hepatitis, Entamoeba histolytica, and Echinococcus was negative. Abdominal ultrasound showed a well-circumscribed 83 mm × 80 mm heterogeneously echoic, solid-appearing mass in the right hepatic lobe with small peripheral anechoic cystic foci and no intralesional vascularity on color Doppler ( ). Computed tomography (CT) revealed a hypodense lesion without internal calcification on noncontrast images, with early arterial enhancement of thin serpiginous peripheral vessels and progressive enhancement of internal septations on postcontrast phases ( ). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated heterogeneous T1 hyperintensity, progressive septal enhancement postgadolinium, hypointense T2 components reflecting hemorrhage or myxoid matrix, and occasional fluid-fluid levels ( ). The apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) value of 732 mm²/s is a significant quantitative finding suggesting high cellularity/restricted diffusion, which supports malignancy. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) demonstrated restricted diffusion within the lesion, with an ADC value of 732 mm²/s ( b -value 800 s/mm²), a finding consistent with high tumor cellularity and supportive of malignancy ( ). The case was discussed at a multidisciplinary team meeting, where differentials included Mesenchymal Hamartoma of the liver (MHL), Mucinous Cystic Neoplasm (Biliary cystadenoma, biliary cystadenocarcinoma) and Hepatic Hydatid disease. Due to the lesion’s size, complexity, and concern for malignancy, the MDT recommended upfront surgical resection without percutaneous biopsy to avoid tumor seeding. Although a laparoscopic approach was initially considered, an open right hemihepatectomy was ultimately performed due to concerns regarding potential cyst rupture. Intraoperatively, a large cystic–solid mass was identified within the right hemiliver, with no evidence of peritoneal disease. The procedure was undertaken using combined Glissonean and anterior approaches. The gallbladder was removed to facilitate exposure. Both the right anterior and right posterior Glissonean pedicles were carefully dissected and transected separately using 35-mm Echelon vascular staplers, with the staple lines reinforced using 5-0 PDS sutures. Parenchymal transection was performed in the standard manner with CUSA, Harmonic scalpel, ligaclips, Hem-o-lok clips, Vicryl ties, and 4-0 Prolene sutures, following the demarcation line to the anterior surface of the inferior vena cava. The right hepatic vein was subsequently divided with a 35-mm Echelon vascular stapler. Right liver mobilization was completed by dividing the triangular and coronary ligaments and separating the liver from the inferior vena cava while preserving the right adrenal gland. The specimen was removed, and the hepatic resection surface was treated with Tisseel prior to completion of the procedure ( ). Histopathology confirmed UESL, showing spindle or stellate cells in a fibromyxoid background with pleomorphic giant cells ( ) and diastase-resistant periodic acid-Schiff-positive eosinophilic globules ( ). On immunohistochemistry, the tumor cells were positive for markers of mesenchymal origin: vimentin ( ) and alpha-1-antitrypsin ( ). Additional positive markers included CD10 ( ), CD68 ( ), Bcl-2 ( ), and CKAE1/3 ( ). The tumor cells were negative for CD117, DOG1, CD34, ERG, S100, SOX10, Melan-A, HMB45, OCT3/4, SALL4, PLAP, HepPar1, AFP, desmin, myogenin, Myo-D1, ALK1, ROS1, CD21, CD23 and CD35. The variable expression of histiocytic, mesenchymal, and epithelial markers suggests primitive stem cell origin of this lesion. Postoperatively, the patient made an uncomplicated recovery and was discharged on postoperative day 5. Discussion Diagnosis of UESL is challenging due to its paradoxical imaging features: solid or heterogeneous on ultrasound, but cystic or complex solid-cystic with septations, hemorrhage, and variable enhancement on CT and MRI [ , , , ]. In this case, the discrepancy between ultrasound (solid with peripheral anechoic foci) and CT/MRI (predominantly cystic with enhancing septations and serpiginous vessels) is typical. MRI provided additional insights, such as T1 hyperintense/T2 hypointense zones indicating intratumoral hemorrhage and myxoid content, and fluid-fluid levels. Although not pathognomonic, a large hepatic mass in a young adult with normal biochemistry and tumor markers, combined with discordant imaging, should raise suspicion for UESL. Differentiation from other cystic lesions (eg, mucinous cystic neoplasm, hydatid cyst, hematoma, pyogenic abscess) is essential ( ). Percutaneous biopsy is often avoided due to seeding risks and low yield in myxoid lesions. Upfront resection, as performed here, enabled histological confirmation of classic UESL features. UESL presents a well-recognized diagnostic challenge owing to its paradoxical cross-modal imaging appearance. In the present case, abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a solid or heterogeneously echoic mass, while CT and MRI characterized it as a predominantly cystic lesion with enhancing internal septations, thin serpiginous peripheral vessels, and T1-hyperintense/T2-hypointense foci reflecting intratumoral hemorrhage and myxoid matrix. This discordance—solid on ultrasound yet cystic on CT and MRI—is regarded as the cardinal imaging feature of UESL and arises because the myxoid, gelatinous tumor content attenuates ultrasound waves differently from its true internal composition [ , , , ]. Fluid-fluid levels, as observed in this case, further reflect prior intratumoral hemorrhage and are a recognized though nonpathognomonic MRI finding in UESL. DWI demonstrated irregular restricted diffusion within the lesion, with a maximum ADC value of 732 × 10 − ³ mm²/s at b = 800 s/mm². This is significantly lower than the ADC values typically associated with benign cystic lesions (>2.0 × 10 − ³ mm²/s) and is consistent with the high cellular density and myxoid stroma of UESL, supporting malignancy. Although DWI findings in UESL have not been systematically characterized in large series, restricted diffusion in this clinical context strengthens the case for a primary hepatic malignancy. The relationship between UESL and MHL is of pathological and clinical significance. Both entities share chromosomal abnormalities at the 19q13.4 locus, supporting the hypothesis that UESL may arise through malignant transformation of MHL. This genetic continuum means that MHL must be included as an important differential diagnosis in young patients with solid-cystic hepatic lesions, particularly given that distinguishing the two preoperatively on imaging alone may be impossible. In the present case, there were no radiological features favoring MHL—notably the absence of a predominantly cystic, nonenhancing mass without restricted diffusion—and the patient’s age (23 years) was beyond the typical presentation of MHL (under 2 years of age). On histopathological and immunohistochemical evaluation, the diagnosis of UESL was confirmed by the characteristic triad of spindle and stellate cells in a fibromyxoid background, pleomorphic multinucleate giant cells, and diastase-resistant PAS-positive eosinophilic globules ( ). The immunohistochemical profile—diffuse vimentin and α1-antitrypsin positivity, variable CD68 and Bcl-2 expression, focal CKAE1/3, and negativity for lineage-specific markers including HepPar1, AFP, desmin, myogenin, and S100—is consistent with a primitive mesenchymal tumor of undetermined stem cell origin. The focal CKAE1/3 expression, though unexpected in a mesenchymal lesion, has been previously described in UESL and does not exclude the diagnosis. The absence of myogenin and Myo-D1 effectively excludes rhabdomyosarcoma, and negativity for CD117 and DOG1 excludes gastrointestinal stromal tumor with hepatic involvement. The decision to proceed with upfront surgical resection without percutaneous biopsy was appropriate and consistent with current management principles. Biopsy of complex cystic or myxoid lesions carries a risk of tumor seeding along the needle tract, and the diagnostic yield in heavily myxoid tumors is low due to sampling of nonrepresentative gelatinous material. The decision to proceed with upfront surgical resection without percutaneous biopsy was appropriate and consistent with current management principles. Biopsy of complex cystic or myxoid lesions carries a risk of tumor seeding along the needle tract, and the diagnostic yield in heavily myxoid tumors is low due to sampling of nonrepresentative gelatinous material. In this case, the lesion’s size (>8 cm), complexity, and high index of suspicion for malignancy on multimodal imaging collectively supported resection as both the diagnostic and therapeutic intervention. The patient underwent a right hemi hepatectomy via Glissonean and anterior approaches. The Glissonean approach enables extrahepatic control of hepatic inflow pedicles, and the anterior approach avoids tumor mobilization prior to parenchymal transection, minimizing the risk of intrahepatic dissemination. Complete surgical resection (R0) is the cornerstone of treatment for UESL, and its importance in determining prognosis cannot be overstated. In a pooled analysis of 308 patients, Wu et al reported a 5-year overall survival of 65.8% in patients treated with surgery combined with chemotherapy, compared with significantly inferior outcomes in those undergoing surgery alone (1-year survival 93% vs 65%; 3-year survival 81% vs 51%). Adults demonstrate lower 5-year survival than children (48.2% vs 84.4%), likely reflecting delayed diagnosis and larger tumor size at presentation [ , , , , ]. The adjuvant chemotherapy regimen employed in this case—ifosfamide and epirubicin—draws from soft tissue sarcoma protocols. Emerging evidence suggests that ifosfamide-containing regimens may have superior efficacy in adult UESL compared to the vincristine/actinomycin D/cyclophosphamide regimens used in paediatric practice, though prospective data are lacking. Recurrence risk remains substantial in adults, with a median time to relapse of approximately 12 months, underscoring the necessity of close postoperative surveillance. The 12-month disease-free outcome observed in the present case is therefore an encouraging but not yet definitive result, and continued follow-up beyond the 24-month mark is essential. The differentials considered at multidisciplinary team review—mesenchymal hamartoma, mucinous cystic neoplasm, and hepatic hydatid disease—represent the most clinically relevant entities in this demographic and are summarized in . In this patient, negative echinococcal serology and absent daughter cysts or peri-cyst calcification effectively excluded hydatid disease. Mucinous cystic neoplasm was considered but regarded as less likely given the patient’s age (typically middle-aged women) and right lobe location (MCN predominates in the left lobe/segment IV). The cross-modal imaging discordance, normal tumor markers, young age, and ultimately the histopathology together confirmed UESL as the diagnosis. This case underscores that awareness of UESL’s radiological hallmarks—cross-modal discordance, enhancing septations, serpiginous peripheral vascularity, intertumoral hemorrhage, fluid-fluid levels, and restricted diffusion—is critical to avoiding misdiagnosis and facilitating timely multidisciplinary surgical planning. This case illustrates that UESL should be considered in the differential diagnosis of any large, complex hepatic mass in a young adult, even in the absence of specific laboratory abnormalities or tumor marker elevation. The characteristic cross-modal imaging discordance—a solid or heterogeneous appearance on ultrasound contrasting with a predominantly cystic, septate morphology on CT and MRI—is the single most diagnostically useful feature of this entity and should prompt early multidisciplinary discussion. Awareness of this paradox is critical to avoiding the reported misdiagnosis rate of up to 23.5%. Complete surgical resection remains the cornerstone of treatment; combined with adjuvant chemotherapy, multimodal management has been associated with improved survival rates [ ] ( ). In a pooled analysis of 308 patients, Wu et al reported an overall 5-year survival of 65.8%, with 70% for the partial hepatectomy subgroup and 78.9% for liver transplantation recipients [ , , ]. For patients undergoing partial hepatectomy, paediatric age, radical resection, and combined chemotherapy were independent predictors of improved survival [ ]. Adults, however, carry a higher recurrence risk than children, with a median time to relapse of approximately 12 months, underscoring the importance of close, protracted surveillance and prompt re-treatment at recurrence. This case adds to the growing literature supporting upfront resection without percutaneous biopsy and demonstrates a favorable 12-month disease-free outcome following R0 hepatectomy and ifosfamide-based adjuvant chemotherapy in a young adult with localized UESL [ ]. An increasing awareness of i DILI diagnosis and carefully excluding liver damage induced by other causes is the key to a proper diagnosis of i DILI. However, delayed diagnosis, inappropriate monitor and care leads to serious clinical consequences, such as acute liver failure or even liver-related death. In addition, there is presently no effective treatment for i DILI. Herein, we presented the main recommendations of the recent EASL published first DILI guidelines into Chinese language to facilitate liver disease authors and health workers to understand the latest research progress of DILI. 指南 诊断 治疗 药物性肝损伤 Guideline Diagnosis Therapy Drug-induced liver injury pmc-status-qastatus 0 pmc-status-live yes pmc-status-embargo no pmc-status-released yes pmc-prop-open-access no pmc-prop-olf no pmc-prop-manuscript no pmc-prop-legally-suppressed no pmc-prop-has-pdf yes pmc-prop-has-supplement no pmc-prop-pdf-only no pmc-prop-suppress-copyright no pmc-prop-is-real-version no pmc-prop-is-scanned-article no pmc-prop-preprint no pmc-prop-in-epmc yes
